Consonantal i

SearchHow we decideRulings

Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Money, work & business

loan noun

also loans, a loan, lend money, on loan, take out a loan

classical

Cic. Att. 11.3.3: cui magnam dedimus pecūniam mūtuam, to whom I have lent a large sum
Caes. BC 1.39.3: mūtuās pecūniās sūmpsit, he borrowed money

pecūnia mūtua

noun and adjective

money lent or borrowed: a loan

Latin says it with mūtuus, lent: pecūniam mūtuam dare, to lend money, sūmere, to borrow it; comedy says mūtuom argentum (Plaut. Trin. 758). A thing lent to be used and given back is given ūtendum (see borrow).

Examples

  • sī quoi mūtuom quid dederis, fit prō propriō perditum: quom repetās, inimīcum amīcum beneficiō inveniās tuō.

    Lend anybody anything and it is as good as lost: when you ask for it back, you find that your kindness has made your friend an enemy.Plaut. Trin. 1051–1052

  • Age, sequere mē, dabō tibi mūtuō jūglandēs. — Amīcē nunc loqueris. Sed quandō reddam? — Ad Kalendās Graecās, sī nōn potes citius.

    Come on, follow me, I’ll lend you some walnuts. — Now you’re talking like a friend. But when do I give them back? — On the Greek Kalends, if you can’t sooner.Cord. Coll. 2.31

Other words

  • crēditum, crēditī n. — a loan, as the lender sees it

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · Sall. Cat. 25.4: crēditum abjūrāverat, she had denied a loan on oath; Cato Agr. 5.4: injussū dominī crēdat nēminī, let him lend to no one without the master’s leave

    From crēdere, to lend, to trust someone with money (Lewis & Short).

  • mūtuum, mūtuī n. — a loan (the lawyers’ word)

    noun, second declension · also used · post-classical · Gai. Inst. 3.90 (Lewis & Short)

See also borrow, lend, debt, owe, interest, bank.
